Chapter 3: Testing Assumptions and Seeking Contradictory Evidence.
So, you've gathered a bunch of options—what comes next? Well, the real challenge is figuring out how to evaluate them fairly. It's natural to want to stick with information that fits what you already believe. But, that habit—called confirmation bias—can actually trip us up, making us overconfident and sometimes leading to poor decisions.
The antidote? You've got to intentionally test your assumptions and really look for evidence that might prove you wrong.
Picture this: A hiring manager is convinced they've found the perfect candidate. Without even realizing it, they're focusing on the candidate’s strengths and brushing aside the warning signs in references or past performance. To avoid falling into that trap, it's important to make a habit of searching for information that could challenge your first impression.
One smart tactic is to "zoom out" and see how similar choices have worked out for other people. Let's say you're about to launch a new product. Instead of just trusting your own projections, you might look at how similar products did in the market. That kind of outside view is like a reality check—it can reveal risks you might miss if you only look inward.
Here's another practical move: run small tests or pilot programs. Instead of going all-in on a new idea, try it on a small scale first. For example, if you're considering a new sales strategy, roll it out in just one region before taking it nationwide. This way, you learn from real-world feedback and can tweak your plan before making a big commitment.
It can also help to hear from skeptics or people who see things differently. Someone who disagrees or has faced similar decisions in the past might spot issues you never noticed. Maybe ask a trusted colleague to play "devil’s advocate" or chat with someone who’s been down a similar road. They might raise points you hadn't thought of and keep your thinking honest.
If you want to reality-test your assumptions, here are a few strategies you can try:
First, ask yourself, "What would convince me I’m wrong?" Try to pinpoint the specific evidence that would challenge your plan—and then go out and look for it.
Second, compare to base rates. Dig into how often similar choices have worked or failed in the past, instead of just hoping things will be different for you this time.
And finally, run a “premortem.” Imagine your decision has already failed, and work backward to figure out what might have caused that failure.
When you make a habit of testing your assumptions and searching for evidence that contradicts what you want to believe, you steer clear of wishful thinking. Sure, it takes a bit of humility—and a willingness to be proven wrong—but it seriously boosts your chances of success.
